IRC stands for internet relay chat. Think back to aol instant messenger or icq, if you're familiar with any of those instant message systems. It's kind of like that but instead of friends or contacts, you have different channels sort of like subverses. The channels are indicated with a # so there's a main channel for voat called #voat, this channel doesn't really have a theme or area of discussion just more of a free for all. Then you may have channels dedicated to certain topics, like #NFL would be for anyone who wants to talk about NFL or just hang out with other NFL fans and talk about whatever. I can make each one of us mods of that channel so we can manage what goes on in there too. #NFLmods is a channel where we, as mods, can get together and talk in real time so we don't have to keep checking our inbox if we're waiting for a reply. I can also make the channel private so only we can get in.

I would recommend using Kiwi IRC because it's easy to use and you don't really have to mess with any settings or configurations.

To get started, go here: https://kiwiirc.com/client/irc.veuwer.com/#NFLmods For your username use your voat username. Leave the password box unchecked for now and make sure the channel is set to #NFLmods (it should already be there). Click connect and you'll join the channel.

Once you get in the channel, you can register your username so no one else can come in and take your name from you. To do that type the command /ns register password emailaddress with your password and email address you want to use. Commands are typed and sent through the same entry field as sending a message. After you've registered your username (or nick), you will now have to "identify" when you login. That's what the checkbox is for at the login screen, but mine times out when I try to do that so I have to identify my nick in channel by sending the command /ns identify mypassword If you don't identify within a minute or so it will rename you to something random like Guest12345.

There are a lot of other commands in IRC, and a lot of it you just kinda have to learn as you go. It would probably be best to answer your questions as they come to you so it will make a little more sense.

There's a lot of useful information in this link for learning about IRC commands and managing a channel.

What is the proper procedure for dealing with the death of a person attending a funeral?

I don't think there's an all-purpose answer to this question, it would depend on the specific circumstances, who the two deaths were, if it would make sense for them to share a funeral, if all the people who should say good-bye to the second dead person would already be in attendance at the current funeral, etc.

Can't do that, can't just bury the second dead guy at the same funeral. You need to call paramedics and the recently deceased needs to be pronounced dead by a licensed doctor.. if not, there would be no death certificate which means next of kin wouldn't be able to collect insurance or settle the estate or will left.

Also, not having him declared dead by a doctor would lead to an investigation by police.

So tl;dr - you call the paramedics to get the guy who died at the funeral and you carry on with already scheduled funeral.

The passwords your web browser saves for you are not safe at all
This is terrifying. I always wondered if some level of encryption or tokenization was occurring in Chrome. Looks like I know the answer now.
When the passwords are stored, there probably is encryption. However, this is when the password is brought out from storage and put into the text field.
Yeah, unfortunately it looks like it is a problem with every browser, even the newest Edge browser on Windows 10.

Browsers cannot store passwords securely. No matter what they do, if they are able to retrieve a plain text password to paste it into a field, then it's not stored securely. Even if they claim to be storing an encrypted version of your password, they still have the decryption key right there on the same computer.

If you care about the security of an account, don't use any browser's "remember password" feature.

Even if they claim to be storing an encrypted version of your password, they still have the decryption key right there on the same computer.

That's why it's important to choose a strong master password. But I agree, it's much better to use a dedicated password manager like KeePass.
Fortunately this type of attack requires physical access. If you want to be secure against this, just use your home computer for banking and shopping.

If you're using Sync on Firefox or Chrome, if someone could login to your account via this service they would download all that information. They might not need physical access to your home box. Which is why multi-factor authentication is important and us keypass/password safe to store passwords is a more better option.
